planting.note: Root leaf or stem cuttings in spring in very well-drained, gritty succulent mix in full sun to bright light, letting cut ends callus before setting them in soil.

directions: Plant in very well-drained, gritty succulent mix in full sun to bright light, watering only once the soil has dried fully. 'Marpin' is an intergeneric cross of Graptopetalum paraguayense and Echeveria pulidonis that forms short-stemmed rosettes of spoon-shaped, powdery blue-green leaves washed with pink, red, and purple tones that intensify with sun and cool weather. Clusters of small yellow, bell-shaped flowers rise on slender branched stalks in winter and spring. It offsets readily, so older clumps can be divided or propagated from dropped leaves to start new plants.

planting.note: Propagate from leaf or offset cuttings in spring, letting the cut ends callus for a few days before placing them on top of fast-draining succulent mix.

directions: Grow in full sun to bright light in very well-drained, gritty soil, watering sparingly and only when fully dry. A Graptopetalum paraguayense and Echeveria hybrid, 'Helios' forms compact rosettes to about 4-5 inches across of flat, pale green leaves edged in reddish pink, with the pink intensifying under strong light and cooler temperatures. It is named for its bright yellow, star-shaped flowers, which appear in clusters above the foliage. It is a comparatively slow offsetter, so established plants are less commonly found than other graptoverias.

planting.note: Root detached leaves or stem cuttings in spring in gritty, fast-draining mix in full sun to bright light.

directions: Site in full sun to bright light in very well-drained, gritty soil and let the mix dry out completely between waterings. This cross of Graptopetalum paraguayense and Echeveria elegans forms rosettes of thick, light bluish, often pink-tinged leaves with paler margins, covered in a whitish bloom, held at the ends of decumbent or trailing stems up to 6 inches across. It produces offsets on long stalks from the leaf axils, giving mature plants a cascading, multi-rosette habit well suited to hanging containers or raised beds. Avoid overhead watering to protect the delicate powdery coating on the leaves.

planting.note: Separate rooted offset chicks in spring and set them in gritty, fast-draining soil in full sun.

directions: Grow in full sun in lean, gritty, well-drained soil; this species tolerates poor soil and drought once established. Small, tight rosettes about 2 inches across are covered in fine white hairs and take on bronze to deep burgundy flushes in cold weather, returning to green in the growing season. Offsets form freely on short stolons, quickly knitting into a dense mat, and unusual clusters of pink, star-shaped flowers rise above the foliage in midsummer. It is among the more cold-tolerant Sempervivum species, shrugging off snow cover and hard freezes without protection.

planting.note: Divide rooted offsets in spring and plant in gritty, well-drained soil in full sun.

directions: Plant in full sun in gritty, fast-draining soil, watering only occasionally once established. 'Averil' forms rosettes of grey-green, finely fuzzy leaves edged in white cilia that flush shades of red, purple, or chocolate brown depending on the season and light intensity. Like other hens-and-chicks, the mother rosette produces offsets on short stolons that knit into a dense mat over time. It is an easy, reliable hardy succulent for rock gardens, troughs, and green roofs.

planting.note: Divide lateral offsets in spring and set into gritty, well-drained soil in full sun; established mats need little further care.

directions: Grow in full sun in lean, well-drained soil; 'Crispyn' is a compact mat-forming cultivar bred in Belgium by Gustaaf v.d. Steen, with tight rosettes to about 2.5 inches across. The fleshy, pointed leaves are dark purple-red at the tips, sometimes coloring the whole leaf, while the leaf base can stay greener, and the balance shifts with the seasons. In summer a 6-inch flower spike bears starry pink blooms; as with all sempervivums, the flowering rosette then dies but is quickly replaced by offsets on lateral runners. It suits rock gardens, troughs, and alpine rockeries where year-round color is wanted.

planting.note: Divide offsets in spring into gritty, well-drained soil in full sun; this American cultivar is unfussy once established.

directions: Plant in full sun in gritty, fast-draining soil, allowing it to dry between waterings. 'Hepworth Hybrid' bears lightly velvety leaves in a silvery green tone that develop reddish flushing under bright sun stress, with winter frosts bringing out deep purple pigments across the rosette. It spreads by producing offsets on stolons that form a tight, slowly expanding colony. Like other hardy sempervivums, it needs sharp drainage and tolerates extended drought and hard freezes without protection.

planting.note: Take offsets or rooted side shoots in spring and plant in gritty, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade, giving winter protection in colder parts of its range.

directions: Grow in full sun to part shade (useful in hot climates) in gritty, well-drained soil, watering moderately during active growth and sparingly in winter. 'Sienna' is a Sempervivum x Aeonium intergeneric hybrid ('Green Ice' x 'Ice Warrior') raised by the Cornwall nursery Surreal Succulents, forming a mounding plant to around 16 inches tall and wide with a large central rosette surrounded by smaller offsets. Long, lime-green leaves flush bright red in strong sun and cycle through green-purple in autumn to deep burgundy with a green center in late winter. Unlike its Aeonium parent, it does not go dormant, but it has so far only been proven reliably hardy to about 25 degrees F, so it is best given shelter or mulch where winters dip colder.

planting.note: Let a harvested pad callus for about a week in a dry, shaded spot, then set the cut end into very well-drained, gritty soil in full sun in late spring.

directions: Plant a callused pad in sandy, rocky, fast-draining soil in full sun; this hybrid selection between Opuntia fragilis and O. humifusa was named and introduced by Colorado grower Kelly Grummons. It forms a compact, mounding, cushion-like clump of small pads only about 8 inches tall and a foot wide, smaller and tidier than most other cold-hardy opuntias, and bears golden-yellow flowers in June. It is rated hardy through USDA zone 3 and, unlike many western prickly pears, tolerates somewhat more regular moisture without rotting. Its low, dense habit suits small rock gardens, troughs, and tight spaces where larger pricklypears would sprawl too far.

planting.note: Let a harvested pad callus for several days, then set the cut end an inch into sandy or gritty, fast-draining soil in full sun.

directions: Grow in full sun in sandy or loamy, very well-drained soil; Potts' pricklypear is native to dry plains and hills of Arizona, New Mexico, Texas, and northern Mexico. It forms low, spreading clumps of small, rounded to rhombic green pads, with flower color that is notably variable from population to population, ranging from yellow with red centers to pink, red, or orange. Fruit follows as fleshy, egg-shaped tunas. It stays lower and more compact than many of its prickly pear relatives, making it a good choice for small rock gardens and dry slopes.

planting.note: Let a harvested pad callus for about a week, then set the cut end into sandy, gritty, fast-draining soil in full sun.

directions: Plant in full sun in sandy or rocky, well-drained soil; this low, sprawling prickly pear is native across the cold-winter Great Plains, from Wyoming and Nebraska south through Colorado, Kansas, Oklahoma, Texas, and New Mexico. It forms creeping clumps only one to three pads high, with egg- to teardrop-shaped pads that wrinkle under drought or cold stress, armed with slender, often twisted spines (the source of its common name) that range from reddish-brown to white with brown tips. Large golden-yellow flowers with reddish centers appear in late spring, followed by purple-red fruit. Its Great Plains origins make it reliably cold-hardy well beyond what its subtropical-sounding relatives can withstand.

planting.note: Let a harvested pad callus for about a week, then set the cut end into very well-drained, gritty soil in full sun in a sheltered spot.

directions: Grow in full sun in gritty, very well-drained soil; native to south Texas, chenille pricklypear gets its common name from the dense clusters of fine, hair-like golden-yellow to dark red glochids that cover its dull grey-green pads, often with few or no true spines. Established plants can reach 2 to 3 feet tall and wide and produce bright yellow to orange flowers followed by edible purple fruit. It is hardy into USDA zone 8 in well-drained soil but benefits from a dry winter and some shelter where hard freezes are prolonged. Handle pads with gloves and tongs, since the fine glochids embed readily in skin.

planting.note: Root offsets or leaf cuttings in spring in fast-draining, gritty succulent mix in full sun to bright light.

directions: Plant in very well-drained, gritty soil in full sun to bright light, letting the soil dry fully between waterings. 'Blue Sky' is a vigorous, fast-growing echeveria that forms large rosettes of broad, spoon-shaped, powdery blue-green leaves up to 8 inches wide individually, with tips and edges flushing deep pink to red under bright sun and cool temperatures. It offsets freely, building into wide clumps over a foot across, and sends up branched, arching flower stalks bearing clusters of pink blooms in summer. Its quick growth and large scale make it useful for landscape edging and rock gardens in mild climates as well as containers elsewhere.

planting.note: Remove rooted basal offsets in spring and plant in very well-drained, gritty or rocky soil in full sun.

directions: Grow in full sun in lean, gritty, sharply drained soil, watering only occasionally during the growing season and keeping it nearly dry over winter. A genuinely small, slow-growing agave closely related to Agave parryi, it forms a tidy, compact rosette only about 4-6 inches tall that resembles a miniature artichoke, with broad, blue-green leaves edged in a pale margin and tipped with a short terminal spine. It stays compact for years and slowly produces basal offsets rather than suckering widely, making it well suited to rock gardens, troughs, and tight spaces where larger agaves would quickly outgrow their site.

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring in very well-drained, gritty or rocky soil in full sun; this species is solitary and does not produce offsets, so new plants must come from seed or purchased stock.

directions: Site in full sun in gritty, rocky, sharply drained soil and keep nearly dry over winter, since wet, cold soil is the main cause of rot. Native to the Sonoran desert of Mexico, this solitary agave forms a single rosette, eventually reaching up to about 32 inches across, of narrow grey-green leaves tipped with a notably long terminal spine, a feature that distinguishes it from the similar Agave ocahui. Because it never offsets, each plant remains a single clean rosette for its whole life rather than forming a spreading clump. It is hardy to around 10 degrees F and can be grown outdoors through USDA zone 8b with a dry winter site.
